raw_response:
Standing at the edge of my field in early April, thinking through what I need to do this season...

---

I've been at this for 30 years. Used to farm all cotton — this whole area did. But cotton picking wears you out, and the price goes up and down every year. Four or five years back I saw my neighbor Old Zhang making steadier money from stevia. He has a contract with the processing plant in Yongnian, fixed price, they come pick it up. I talked to him a lot, then switched most of my land over. Kept a small cotton plot because I know it well and it spreads my risk a bit — if the stevia company lowers their contract price, I still have something else.

With 7 mouths and two of my sons doing wage work in Handan, the farm can't fail. I'm not trying to get rich off 4.1 mu. I need it to be reliable.

**On stevia (3 mu):** I'll buy cuttings from the village seedling station in late April and transplant them in rows. It's a bit more expensive than buying cheaper cuttings from further away, but local ones establish better — I learned that the hard way my second year. I put down compound fertilizer before transplanting, then topdress with urea after each cut. I cut twice: once in late July, once in late September before frost. The processing plant told me last year that leaf quality matters now, not just weight, so I'm being more careful about timing the cut — not too late or the glycoside content drops. I'll irrigate from the well about four times. My oldest son usually comes home to help with transplanting and the first cut. Without him I'd have to hire someone.

**On cotton (1.1 mu):** I've always grown cotton and I'll keep this small plot. I buy the same hybrid seed from the township supply store — Ruiza 816, it's what everyone around here uses, reliable enough. I plant in late April after the soil warms up. The picking season in September and October is the hardest part — my wife and I do most of it ourselves. I use less fertilizer on cotton now than I used to, maybe 12-13 kg of nitrogen per mu. The extension station said to reduce nitrogen to improve fiber quality and I've noticed it makes sense. I'll spray once or twice for bollworm — that's not optional, you skip it and you lose the crop.

My main worry this year is water cost. Electricity for pumping went up again. I'll irrigate stevia when the leaves start to droop a bit, not on a fixed schedule. That saves maybe 30-40 yuan per mu over the season. Small amount but it adds up.
